\title{Physics-guided machine-learning prediction of spontaneous energy localization in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring}

\author{Adrian Mittal\\[6pt]
{\small Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15213}\\[6pt]
{\small almittal@andrew.cmu.edu}}

\date{}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
In a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a global coupling, a nearly uniform swing is destabilized by a type-III instability and, after several swing periods, concentrates its energy on a few pendulums. In earlier work we predicted where this hotspot forms from early-time data, first by spatial smoothing and then with a convolutional and recurrent neural network. Here we revisit the problem starting from the physics of the instability. The Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing shows that only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, which accounts for the optimal smoothing width found before, and the site is fixed by the initial state, so prediction is limited by measurement precision rather than by chaos. Guided by the spectrum, and testing every choice by ablation, we replace the recurrent network with a small convolutional network built around the ring's symmetry. With a thousandth of the parameters, it halves the error of the earlier network at its stated settings and outperforms it with 60 times less training data; the accuracy reported for that network belongs to a lower localization threshold and smaller initial offsets. Much of the remaining error belongs to the target: the first pendulum to hold 10\% of the energy jitters within a swing, whereas the hump of energy that forms, read when the first pendulum swings over the top, is located within one pendulum in 99.4\% of runs. The inherited settings also enter through the spectrum: localization takes 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode at any amplitude or global coupling, the initial offsets set this clock, and chains at other couplings with matching spectra localize within one pendulum of each other in 88--98\% of runs. We close with what this means for a real chain.
\end{abstract}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Spontaneous energy localization, whereby a significant portion of a nonlinear system's energy gathers on a small part of it, is common in nonlinear lattices \cite{sievers1988intrinsic,campbell2004localizing,flach2008discrete}. Because such ``hotspots'' may also matter in structures from micromechanical arrays to bridges and transmission lines \cite{sato2006colloquium,green2006failure,ARIOLI2015901,zhang2017wind}, predicting where they form is of practical as well as fundamental interest. A well-known pathway to localization is the modulational instability of a plane-wave mode \cite{kivshar1993creation,dauxois1993energy,extreme}, and an instability of type III \cite{cross1993pattern}, which amplifies the longest waves, often leads to catastrophic localization \cite{english2003modulational,thakur2007driven,cuevas2009discrete}. Since the instability is seeded by noise, where the energy localizes depends sensitively on the initial conditions.

In a previous paper \cite{mittal2026jand} we studied this problem numerically in the discrete sine-Gordon model \cite{cuevas2014sine}, realized as a ring of torsionally coupled pendulums with a global coupling that selects an instability of type III. Smoothing the early energy profile with a box-car of about 17 pendulums substantially improved predictions of the localization site, suggesting that the instability is sensitive to energetic clusters rather than to single pendulums. We then reported that a convolutional neural network combined with a bidirectional long short-term memory network \cite{Hochreiter1997} (CNN-BiLSTM) located the site within $\pm1$ pendulum in 94.4\% of test cases. We concluded that the network had found features beyond energy clusters, and that a future study should aim at teasing them out.

The present paper is that study. Rather than treat the predictor as a black box, we begin with the linear stability of the uniform swing, its Floquet growth spectrum, and ask what it implies for each design question: what to measure, what architecture to use, and how to train it. For each question we stated a hypothesis before running the experiment, grounded in the spectrum wherever the physics had something to say, in the spirit of physics-informed machine learning \cite{karniadakis2021physics}, and tested it with an ablation, a controlled comparison that could refute it. We also wanted a predictor that is efficient and easy to implement, small enough to train in minutes on a laptop and fed with measurements that a real chain could provide. We report the choices that did not pay off alongside those that did.

Three findings stand out. First, only a handful of the longest ring modes are unstable, and this explains the smoothing width of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. Second, a network that sees the whole ring and treats every pendulum alike halves the error of the CNN-BiLSTM with a thousandth of the parameters. Third, much of the remaining error belongs to the label, because the first pendulum to cross the 10\% threshold of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} jitters within a swing; defined at the scale of the hump of energy that forms, and timed by the first pendulum to swing over the top, the site becomes almost fully predictable. Beyond these, the settings taken over from Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the amplitude, the size of the initial offsets and the global coupling, enter almost entirely through the growth spectrum, which sets both when and, to within a pendulum, where the energy localizes. A longer ring adds competing modes at little cost in accuracy.

One point applies throughout. Retrained at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a localization threshold of 10\% of the total energy and initial offsets of $\pm0.025$~rad, the CNN-BiLSTM places 60.4\% of test runs within $\pm1$ rather than 94.4\%; the published accuracy was obtained with an effective threshold of 4--5\% of the total energy and offsets of $\pm0.0125$~rad (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}). We compare the two networks, which we call \emph{v1} and \emph{v2}, on the same test runs at the stated settings, and compare both with physics baselines that need no training data.

Section~\ref{sec:methods} introduces the model, its growth spectrum and our methods. Section~\ref{sec:results} presents the results: what the spectrum explains (Sec.~\ref{sec:physics}), the design of the network (Secs.~\ref{sec:arch}--\ref{sec:final}), the choice of target (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}), how the settings enter (Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}) and what a real chain requires (Sec.~\ref{sec:realchain}). Section~\ref{sec:conclusions} concludes, and Appendix~\ref{sec:repro} identifies the settings behind the accuracy published for v1.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

\subsection{The pendulum ring}

We consider the same system as in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}: a ring of $N$ pendulums with torsional nearest-neighbor coupling and a global coupling to the chain average. In dimensionless time $\tau=\omega_0 t$, with $\omega_0^2=g/l$, the angles obey
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eom}
\ddot\theta_n = -\sin\theta_n + \gt\,(\theta_{n+1}+\theta_{n-1}-2\theta_n) + \htl\,(\bar\theta-\theta_n),
\end{equation}
where $\bar\theta$ is the mean angle over the ring, indices are taken modulo $N$, and the dot denotes $d/d\tau$. We use $N=100$, $\gt=0.75$ and $\htl=0.5$.\footnote{Section~2.1 of the journal version of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} prints $\htl=0.05$, a typographical error: Sec.~2.3 there and the simulation code use $\htl=0.5$, the value that gives the instability threshold near $A=1.59$ reported there (our Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}).} Each run starts at rest with $\theta_n(0)=A+\eta_n$, where the amplitude $A\sim\mathcal{U}(1.65,1.85)$ is drawn once per run and the offsets $\eta_n\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.025,0.025)$ independently for every pendulum. The energy of site $n$ is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:energy}
E_n = \tfrac12\dot\theta_n^2 + (1-\cos\theta_n) + \tfrac{\gt}{2}(\theta_{n+1}-\theta_n)^2 + \tfrac{\htl}{2}(\theta_n-\bar\theta)^2 ,
\end{equation}
which assigns to each pendulum the spring to its right-hand neighbor, as in the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand};\footnote{Equation~(5) of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} prints the spring to the left-hand neighbor. The statistics are the same by symmetry, but the labeled site can differ.} the total energy $\Etot=\sum_n E_n$ is conserved. After swinging almost uniformly for several tens of time units, about 57 on average, the ring suddenly concentrates its energy in a hump several pendulums wide, and one pendulum holds more than 10\% of the total, ten times its equipartition share. For pendulums 20~cm long this happens about 8~s after release. We ask how well the early behavior of the ring predicts which pendulum this will be.

\subsection{Linear stability of the uniform swing}
\label{sec:floquet}

Without offsets, every pendulum follows the same swing $\Theta(\tau)$, with $\ddot\Theta=-\sin\Theta$, $\Theta(0)=A$ and $\dot\Theta(0)=0$, whose period is $T(A)=4\mathcal{K}(k)$, $\mathcal{K}$ being the complete elliptic integral of the first kind of modulus $k=\sin(A/2)$. Writing $\theta_n=\Theta+\delta\theta_n$ and expanding the perturbation in ring modes, $\delta\theta_n=\sum_m a_m(\tau)\,e^{2\pi i mn/N}$, we linearize Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) and obtain for every mode $m\ge1$ a Hill equation \cite{magnus1966hill},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hill}
\ddot a_m + \left[\cos\Theta(\tau) + \htl + 4\gt\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi m}{N}\right)\right] a_m = 0 ,
\end{equation}
whose coefficient repeats every half swing, $T(A)/2$, so that the swing drives each mode parametrically \cite{landau1976mechanics}. The global term adds the same stiffness $\htl$ to every mode except the uniform one, which is the swing itself; this shift selects an instability of type III \cite{cross1993pattern,mittal2026jand}, in which the longest waves grow first and fastest. Integrating Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) over one swing period $T(A)$ gives the $2\times2$ monodromy matrix $M_m(A)$, whose eigenvalue of largest modulus, $\mu_m$, defines the growth rate $\sigma_m(A)=\ln|\mu_m(A)|/T(A)$; mode $m$ grows when $\sigma_m>0$.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig1_spectrum.pdf}
  \caption{Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing, Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}). (a)~Growth rate $\sigma_m$ of ring mode $m$ (wavelength $100/m$ pendulums) against the swing amplitude $A$; the swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$, and the bar marks the amplitudes in the data. (b)~At $A=1.75$ only modes $m=1$--$5$ grow; the labels give the $e$-folding time of each mode.}
  \label{fig:spectrum}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:spectrum} shows the resulting spectrum. The uniform swing becomes unstable at $A_c=1.577$, consistent with the vertical asymptote of the localization time near $A=1.59$ found numerically in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. As the amplitude increases, more long waves become unstable, but only a few do in the range used here: at $A=1.75$ only the five longest waves grow, with wavelengths of 100, 50, 33, 25 and 20 pendulums. The fastest grows by a factor of $e$ every 8.4 time units, so during the first 4.5 time units after release, the observation window of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the perturbation grows by less than a factor of two.

Three expectations follow, and they guide everything below. First, since the growing modes are the longest waves of the ring, the eventual site should be a property of the whole ring rather than of a local neighborhood. Second, since so little growth occurs in the observation window, a predictor must essentially read the initial perturbation and project it onto the growing modes, rather than watch the hotspot form. Third, little else happens in time during that window: a small-amplitude estimate of the largest group velocity gives about half a pendulum per time unit, so a disturbance moves by only about two pendulums. Moreover, since the ring is released from rest, the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$ are its complete state, and everything observed later is a function of them.

\subsection{Simulation, labels and metrics}
\label{sec:pools}

Training some 760 networks requires far more simulated runs than Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} did, so we replaced its run-by-run \texttt{odeint} integration \cite{virtanen2020scipy} with a fourth-order Runge--Kutta scheme \cite{press1992numerical} that integrates thousands of runs at once (step $\Delta\tau=0.05$; samples every 0.5 time units, as before). On 1,000 test runs it gives exactly the same localization site and time as the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, more than ten times faster. Models are trained on up to 100,000 runs, the first 60,000 matching the training budget of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}; a validation pool of 20,000 runs serves for every model choice, and a test pool of 20,000 runs only for the numbers we report. The pools are generated with different random seeds, so no run appears in two of them, and inputs are standardized with statistics of the training pool alone. Sections~\ref{sec:settings} and \ref{sec:realchain} use further pools of 75,000 runs at fixed amplitudes, at other global couplings and on rings of other sizes, test pools of 10,000 runs at other amplitudes and couplings and on rings of 80 and 150 pendulums, and the runs of the main pools with their offsets rescaled. In these pools, labels were searched up to $\tau=300$, except on rings of 400 pendulums, where each block of 1,000 runs was integrated only until all its event-timed labels (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}) were complete.

Following Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, a run localizes at the first sample at which one site holds more than 10\% of the total energy, $\max_n E_n>0.1\,\Etot$, and its label is that site. We call this the \emph{first-crossing label} and, with the offsets above, use it for every comparison with v1, since these are the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}); Sec.~\ref{sec:target} introduces smoother labels and examines the choice of threshold. Distances are measured around the ring, $d(n,n')=\min(|n-n'|,\,N-|n-n'|)$. Accuracy within $\pm1$, the metric of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, was chosen there because the localized energy spans several pendulums, a point that Sec.~\ref{sec:target} bears out; it also partly rewards a convention, since in 19\% of test runs, which pendulum crosses first changes if the spring energy in Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}) is split evenly between neighbors. We therefore also report the mean distance between predicted and true site, the accuracy within $\pm3$, and the share of runs more than 10 sites off, which we call far misses. The test pool resolves an accuracy to a standard error of 0.3 percentage points.

\subsection{Predictors and protocol}
\label{sec:predictors}

We compare the networks with three physics baselines. The \emph{box-car} predictor of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} picks the site where a moving average of the site energy peaks, with the width and the time of the snapshot chosen on the validation pool. The \emph{Floquet filter} needs no training at all: it evolves the mean-subtracted initial angles through the linearized dynamics for a whole number of swing periods chosen on the validation pool (six on the main pools, and three to 15 on the pools of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, chosen for each amplitude bin where the pools are binned), multiplying each ring mode by its response computed from $M_m(A)$ at the run's amplitude estimated as the mean of its initial angles, and picks the site where the result peaks. The \emph{linear ring filter} is the simplest trained model that respects the ring, a multinomial logistic regression whose score at each site is a circular convolution of the initial angles over the whole ring, with amplitude-dependent weights (200 parameters); it is convex, and we fit it to its global optimum with L-BFGS \cite{liu1989limited}. The network of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, v1, takes the site energies at $\tau=0,0.5,\dots,4.5$, each frame paired with the initial angles $\theta_n(0)$, and combines per-frame convolutions with a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) layer (Sec.~\ref{sec:arch}). It has 26.5 million parameters, and we retrained it in PyTorch \cite{paszke2019pytorch} with the architecture and training procedure of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} (Appendices~\ref{app:training} and \ref{sec:repro}).

The study proceeded question by question. We first compared architectures, with v1's inputs, then the inputs, the loss and the optimizer, changing one choice at a time; finally we combined the best choices and removed them again one at a time to see which mattered. Inputs, losses and optimizers were compared in shorter screening runs with up to three training seeds (random initializations of the network), the final model with five; training details are given in Appendix~\ref{app:training}.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{What the growth spectrum explains}
\label{sec:physics}

Let us first return to the box-car smoothing of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, whose best width, 17 pendulums, was found empirically. A box-car of width $K$ first cancels the ring mode $m=N/K$; a wider box-car also suppresses longer waves, and a narrower one lets shorter ones through. The best width should therefore cancel the first stable mode, $m_c$, while canceling none of the growing ones, which gives $K^*=N/m_c$, or $100/6\approx17$ at $A=1.75$, where modes 1--5 grow. Figure~\ref{fig:physics}(a) shows that this prediction follows the best width measured at seven amplitudes, from just above threshold to $A=1.90$. The energetic clusters identified in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} thus appear to be the growing long waves, seen through a low-pass filter.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig2_physics.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~The best box-car width (dots, with 16--84\% bootstrap ranges; 2,000 runs per amplitude) follows the Floquet band edge $K^*=N/m_c$ (line), where $m_c$ is the first stable mode; the empirical optimum of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} lies on it. (b)~Share of labels moved by more than one or three sites when white noise of the given size is added to the initial angles; diamonds give the share moved by more than one site when a $10^{-3}$~rad error is placed only in modes $m\le5$ or only in $m\ge6$. (c)~Share of labels moved by more than three sites when the initial perturbation keeps only the modes $m\le M$, or loses the modes $m\le5$.}
  \label{fig:physics}
\end{figure}

Since the localization is seeded by the small offsets of the release, one may ask next whether chaos limits how well it can be predicted. Figure~\ref{fig:physics}(b) shows that it does not. Perturbing the initial angles by $10^{-6}$~rad never changes the label, and neither does halving the integration step, so the label is a deterministic function of the initial state and the best possible accuracy is close to 100\%. What limits prediction is how precisely that state is known: an error of $10^{-3}$~rad on every pendulum moves a quarter of the labels by more than one site, and placed only in the five longest modes, it moves half of them. Conversely [Fig.~\ref{fig:physics}(c)], deleting every initial mode except the five longest keeps the site within $\pm3$ in 91\% of runs, whereas deleting those five makes the site random. The coarse answer thus lives in about ten numbers, the amplitudes and phases of the five growing modes, while local detail decides the last site or two.

Simple physics-based predictors already do well (Table~\ref{tab:headline}). The best box-car reaches a mean distance of 5.07 sites, close to the 5.4 reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. The Floquet filter, which simply grows the measured initial perturbation and has no trained parameters, matches the mean distance of v1 (3.12 against 3.14), although it is less often within $\pm1$. The 200-parameter linear ring filter beats v1 on every metric. These baselines set the bar that any network has to clear.

\subsection{A network built around the ring}
\label{sec:arch}

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \input{fig_schematic}
  \caption{The two networks. (a)~v1 applies four convolutions to each frame separately, so that each feature sees nine neighboring pendulums of one frame, and combines the frames in a bidirectional LSTM whose input is each frame flattened into 25,600 numbers. (b)~v2 stacks the ten angle frames as channels of a signal on the ring, so that every kernel sees all frames at once; seven circular convolutions with growing dilation let every pendulum see the whole ring, and the same small head scores every pendulum.}
  \label{fig:schematic}
\end{figure}

The network of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, designed before the growth spectrum was known, follows a pattern common in networks for video: features are extracted from each frame separately, and a recurrent layer then follows how they change from frame to frame [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(a)]. The spectrum changed what we expected a network for this problem to need. The coarse answer lives in the projection of the initial state onto a few long waves that span the whole ring, while little grows or travels in the 4.5 time units observed (Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}), so the network needs a view of the whole ring more than a model of the sequence of frames. Moreover, since the ring has no ends and the dynamics are the same at every pendulum, the network can wrap around the ring and apply the same filters everywhere, giving one score per site. In v1, by contrast, the global view came from the LSTM's input weights, which are tied to particular pendulums and hold 26.2 of its 26.5 million parameters. These considerations underlie the design of Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b): the ten frames are stacked as input channels, so that every kernel sees all of them at once, and a stack of circular convolutions gives every pendulum a view of the whole ring with a few tens of thousands of parameters. We tested each of these choices separately, with v1's inputs and training budget.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig4_ring.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~Mean test distance of a dilated circular CNN against its receptive field; the line is the 200-parameter linear ring filter. (b)~Mean test distance against the number of training runs for the two-branch network described in the text (shallow circular convolutions plus a global branch on the lowest ring modes) with one score per site, the same with zero padding, and with a v1-style flatten and dense head; the diamond is v1, trained on 60,000 runs. Zero padding costs far less here than in the final model (Table~\ref{tab:choices}), presumably because the global branch is periodic whatever the padding.}
  \label{fig:ring}
\end{figure}

The receptive field, the stretch of the ring that a pendulum's features see, matters most [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(a)]. In a circular CNN of four to seven layers with kernels of three sites, spreading the three sites further apart from layer to layer (dilation) widens the receptive field from 9 to 129 sites, and the mean distance falls from 4.79 to 1.54. A network that sees only nine pendulums is worse even than the linear ring filter, which sees the whole ring.

Our first design, the two-branch network, reached the whole ring differently. Since the linear growth stage multiplies each ring mode by its own factor, we combined a shallow local branch of circular convolutions with a global branch that multiplies each of the lowest ring modes by a learned complex matrix mixing the channels, a generalization of the Floquet response and the form of Fourier neural operators \cite{li2021fourier}. The global branch saturates once it includes the unstable band, as expected, but the deep whole-ring CNN does better still and gains nothing from it, presumably because deciding which of several growing humps wins is a nonlinear competition across the ring that no linear filter captures.

The ring's symmetry, in turn, saves data [Fig.~\ref{fig:ring}(b)]. A network that scores every site with the same filters needs to learn each pattern only once \cite{cohen2016group}; trained on 1,000 runs, the two-branch network with one score per site already beats its flatten-and-dense counterpart trained on 60,000.

Whether the frames still need a recurrent layer was a closer question than we had expected. A small gated recurrent unit (GRU) \cite{cho2014learning} applied to each pendulum's convolved frames helped the two-branch network, lowering its mean distance from 1.75 to 1.59, but not the whole-ring CNN, which scores 1.54 with stacked frames and 1.57 with the GRU in front. On the validation pool the whole-ring CNN ties with the same network plus the global branch and with the two-branch network plus the GRU, and we chose the simplest of the three, the whole-ring CNN without recurrence.

Feeding the network the field evolved by the Floquet filter, which we expected to leave it only the nonlinear correction to learn, did not help even with only 3,000 training runs; the network learns the linear growth stage from the data alone. Nor does the network need to be large: versions of the two-branch network from 2,000 to 115,000 parameters all land within about a third of a site of each other, as one would expect if the answer lives in about ten numbers plus local texture. We did not pursue other families of models: on a ring with nearest-neighbor coupling a graph network reduces to a one-dimensional convolution, a transformer over sites lacks the locality of the coupling, and reservoir computing \cite{Chaos_Ott_2017,PhysRevLett_Ott_2018} forecasts trajectories rather than a single outcome.

\subsection{Inputs and training}
\label{sec:inputs}

Energies were the natural input for v1, since the box-car analysis and the label of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are stated in terms of energy. They hold no information beyond the angles, velocities and coupling constants they are computed from, however, and at release, to first order in the offsets, $E_n(0)$ is a shifted, rescaled copy of $\theta_n(0)$. Energies are also expensive to measure, since velocities call for a gyroscope on every pendulum or noisy differencing of video frames, whereas one camera can track every angle. And $\theta_n(0)$ alone is the complete state (Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}). We therefore expected the initial angles alone to match v1's inputs, and they did; frames of angles did better still, in screening runs of the whole-ring CNN (mean distances of 1.56 for ten angle frames, 1.66 for the initial angles alone, and 1.75 for v1's inputs) and on the cleaner labels of Sec.~\ref{sec:target}, since the later frames, though carrying no new information, make the same information easier to learn. Energies help when the observation starts at an unknown point in the swing, along which they barely change; angles then need about a full swing of frames to do as well.

For the loss, v1 used plain cross-entropy over the 100 sites, which counts a prediction one site off as just as wrong as one 50 sites off. Since neighboring sites are nearly equivalent at the level of the label (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}), we expected soft labels \cite{szegedy2016rethinking}, here spread over the neighbors of the true site, to help, and they did, lowering the mean distance in the same screening runs from 1.75 to 1.58 and cutting the spread between seeds fourfold. Contrary to our expectation, however, they also lower the share of exact hits (from 40\% to 28\% in full-length training). Regressing a position on the ring did worst, because it averages two competing humps into a site between them, and a term for the expected ring distance did not help and made the model hedge at larger weights; we kept a small weight, with which the time head was tested. Since the same growing modes set both when and where the energy localizes, we added a head that predicts the localization time, and it helped the site prediction slightly. The binary head of v1, which predicts whether a run localizes at all, adds nothing on undamped chains, where every run localizes. The optimizer, finally, is a question the physics does not answer: every adaptive optimizer and schedule we tried landed within the spread between seeds, and we kept AdamW \cite{loshchilov2019decoupled} with a cosine schedule \cite{loshchilov2017sgdr}.

\subsection{The final model}
\label{sec:final}

The final model [Fig.~\ref{fig:schematic}(b)] feeds the ten angle frames of Sec.~\ref{sec:inputs}, taken over the observation window of v1, to the whole-ring CNN of Sec.~\ref{sec:arch}: seven circular convolutions of 32 channels with kernels of three sites, at dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 1 \cite{yu2016multiscale,oord2016wavenet}. A small head, the same at every pendulum, gives a score $z_n$ per site and the probability $p_n=e^{z_n}/\sum_{n'}e^{z_{n'}}$, and a second head, linear in the ring-averaged features, predicts the logarithm of the localization time $\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}$. With $y$ the true site, the loss is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:loss}
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_n q_n\ln p_n + \lambda_d\sum_n p_n\, d(n,y) + \lambda_t\left(\hat\ell-\ell\right)^2,
\qquad q_n\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{d(n,y)^2}{2w^2}\right],
\end{equation}
that is, cross-entropy against soft labels of width $w=1$ site, plus $\lambda_d=0.1$ times the expected ring distance, plus $\lambda_t=0.1$ times the squared error of the predicted log-time $\hat\ell$, where $\ell=(\ln\tau_{\mathrm{loc}}-\ln57)/0.2$. The model has 22,786 parameters, none of them tied to a particular pendulum, and trains in about six minutes on the same 60,000 runs as v1.

Table~\ref{tab:headline} compares it with v1 and the baselines. Against v1, v2 halves the mean distance, from 3.14 to 1.49, cuts the far misses from 5.7\% to 1.5\%, and raises the share within $\pm1$ from 60\% to 77\%. It does so with about a thousandth of the parameters and a quarter of the training time. Neither network reaches the 94.4\% within $\pm1$ reported in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, which was obtained at a lower threshold and smaller offsets (Sec.~\ref{sec:target} and Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}).

We then retrained the final model with one choice reverted at a time, and Table~\ref{tab:choices} pairs each choice with the reason it was made. The three architectural choices that the ring's physics dictates matter most. Seeing the whole ring is worth 1.1 sites, circular padding 0.9, and one score per site 0.3, the last while cutting the model's parameters tenfold. Once the architecture is right, v1's inputs and optimizer cost little. The loss matters mainly for the share within $\pm1$: with plain cross-entropy that share falls from 77\% to 64\%, for a reason we shall see in Sec.~\ref{sec:target}.

The network is also economical with data: trained on only 1,000 runs, v2 already beats v1 trained on 60,000 (2.42 against 3.14). Because no parameter is tied to a particular pendulum, it barely overfits, scoring 1.49 on the test pool against 1.35 on its training runs with no dropout \cite{srivastava2014dropout} and only a small weight decay, whereas v1 overfits despite dropout and early stopping (3.00 against 1.62 for one seed). Where v2 does overfit, with little data, dropout and weight decay do not help on their own; what helps is adding the mirror images of the training runs, the one symmetry of the ring that the network does not build in, which is worth about twice the data.

\subsection{What to predict}
\label{sec:target}

Most of v2's remaining error on the first-crossing label turns out to belong to the label. Within one swing, the energy of a forming hotspot changes form and shifts between neighboring pendulums, as we show below, so which pendulum first crosses 10\% depends on the moment in the swing at which the threshold is passed. To average this out, we define a \emph{swing-averaged label}: we split each spring's energy evenly between the two pendulums it joins, which gives a symmetric site energy $E^{\mathrm{s}}_n$, and average it over the last 16 samples, about one swing,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:avg}
\bar E_n(\tau_k) = \frac{1}{16}\sum_{j=0}^{15} E^{\mathrm{s}}_n(\tau_{k-j}) ;
\end{equation}
the label is the top site at the first sample at which $\max_n\bar E_n>0.1\,\Etot$. The two labels agree exactly in only a third of the test runs, the averaged one usually sitting one to three sites to the left [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(a)]. The jitter shows up in the errors, too. Trained with plain cross-entropy, v2 misses by two sites more often than by one, and half of those two-site misses sit exactly on the swing-averaged position [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(b)]. Soft labels hedge between the two candidate sites, which is why they raise the share within $\pm1$ so much.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig5_jitter.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~Swing-averaged site minus first-crossing site on the test pool. (b)~Prediction errors of v2 trained with plain cross-entropy and of the final model (soft labels), both on the first-crossing label, and of the same recipe trained and scored on the swing-averaged label.}
  \label{fig:jitter}
\end{figure}

This raises a more basic question: is a single pendulum the right target at all? When the first-crossing label fires, the top pendulum holds 10.3\% of the energy at that instant but only 5.5\% averaged over a swing, and the swing-averaged hump is about eight pendulums wide at half height. The 10\% on a single pendulum is thus the instantaneous peak of a breathing hump. The hump stays in place for about a swing after it forms, then drifts. At the first crossing of 10\%, about one run in six has a rival hump at least five sites away that holds at least half as much energy, so that any single-site answer is a guess between two places. We therefore also define the label at the scale of the hump. The \emph{hump label} fires at the first sample at which
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hump}
\max_n H_n > 0.15\,\Etot , \qquad H_n = \bar E_{n-1} + \bar E_n + \bar E_{n+1} ,
\end{equation}
and names the center of that three-pendulum window. Its threshold of 15\% was chosen so that it fires together with the first-crossing label, at a median of 54.5 against 55 time units, whereas the swing-averaged label fires about five time units later; below, we replace this threshold with a physical event.

\begin{table}[t]
  \centering
  \caption{The same recipe trained and scored on each label (test pool; seeds in brackets). The event-timed hump label, defined at the end of Sec.~\ref{sec:target}, is the recommended target. Accuracies in \%.}
  \label{tab:labels}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
    \toprule
    Model & Label [seeds] & Mean dist. & Exact & $\pm1$ & $>10$ off \\
    \midrule
    v2 & First crossing [5] & 1.49 & 27.7 & 77.2 & 1.5 \\
    v2 & Swing-averaged [3] & 0.58 & 70.5 & 96.4 & 0.7 \\
    v2 & Hump [3] & 0.27 & 84.7 & 99.4 & 0.4 \\
    v2 & \textbf{Event-timed hump [3]} & \textbf{0.28} & \textbf{86.2} & \textbf{99.4} & \textbf{0.4} \\
    \midrule
    v1 & First crossing [2] & 3.14 & 22.5 & 60.4 & 5.7 \\
    v1 & Swing-averaged [2] & 2.25 & 42.0 & 83.6 & 4.4 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

We trained and scored the same recipe on each label (Table~\ref{tab:labels}). On the swing-averaged label v2 reaches a mean distance of 0.58, with 96.4\% within $\pm1$, and on the hump label 0.27, with 99.4\%. Sharing the springs evenly without averaging over a swing does not help, so the jitter comes from the energy moving within each swing, not from how the spring energy is assigned. The hump label's further gain in mean distance over the swing-averaged label comes about equally from being read five time units earlier, while the hump forms, and from naming the center of a three-pendulum window rather than the top pendulum. The first 4.5 time units thus decide where the hump forms: even the model trained on the first-crossing label is within $\pm1$ of the hump label in 91\% of runs.

Since every design choice of Secs.~\ref{sec:arch} and \ref{sec:inputs} was made on the jittery first-crossing label, we repeated the key ones on the cleaner labels. They hold, and seeing the whole ring matters even more: with a four-layer stack that sees only 17 sites (dilations 1, 2, 4 and 1) the mean distance triples on the swing-averaged label and grows more than fivefold on the hump label, against 1.6-fold on the first-crossing label. Soft labels, by contrast, stop mattering, and on the hump label hard labels do slightly better; on a label that does not jitter, the hedge only blurs the answer. The target is therefore best framed as the center of the hump when it forms, with a probability over all pendulums as output.

This leaves the threshold, which the hump label inherits from the first-crossing label, whose 10\% was set ``somewhat arbitrarily'' in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. A scale with physical meaning is the separatrix energy $E_{\mathrm{sep}}=2$, the on-site energy of a pendulum held at the top in Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}). With $\Etot\approx118$ it is 1.7\% of the total, so the 10\% threshold asks one pendulum for about six times $E_{\mathrm{sep}}$. An event that needs no threshold at all is the first pendulum to swing over the top, $|\theta_n|>\pi$, where its libration turns into rotation. It happens at a median of $\tau=50$, close to the first crossing of 3--4\% of the total energy (median lags of $-1.5$ and $+1.5$ time units), and it marks the hump: that pendulum lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center, the site named by the hump label, in 99.1\% of test runs, and the hump label fires after it in every run, a median of five time units later. The first crossing of 10\% comes at about the same time, 5.5 time units after the event, yet v2 places 99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ of the hump label and only 77\% within $\pm1$ of the first-crossing label. To find out why, we used the first-crossing label as a probe of the hump. We recomputed it at thresholds from 3\% to 15\% of the total energy, which moves it from a median of 1.5 time units before the event to 11.5 after it, and trained the final recipe on each with three seeds (Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}).

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig7_threshold.pdf}
  \caption{(a)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ of the first-crossing label on the test pool against the threshold, for v2 (three seeds; mean and standard deviation) and v1 (mean of two trained seeds), both retrained for this study, which is why their scores at 10\% differ slightly from those in Table~\ref{tab:headline}; for the Floquet filter; and for the hump center used as a predictor, shifted by the constant offset that suits each label best on the validation pool (one site at 7--12\%, none otherwise). The tick ``top'' marks the label given by the first pendulum over the top. At 15\%, the 1.1\% of runs whose label has not fired by $\tau=150$ are left out. (b)~Accuracy of v2 within $\pm1$ of its label against the median lag of the label, in time units, after the first pendulum goes over the top: first-crossing labels at 3--15\% (circles), hump labels of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) with windows of three, five and seven pendulums and thresholds of 10\%, 15\% and 20\% (diamonds, placed at the last sample of their one-swing average), and event-timed hump labels with the same windows (stars, which coincide at zero lag; their one-swing average is centered on the event).}
  \label{fig:threshold}
\end{figure}

The sweep shows, first, that what v2 learns from a single-pendulum label is essentially where the hump forms. At every threshold from 3\% to 12\%, its predictions lie within $\pm1$ of the hump center in 90--99\% of runs, and its accuracy on the label is, to within 2.4 points, that of the hump center used as a predictor, shifted by one site at 7--12\%, where the label tends to lie to the right of the center [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(a)]; across all thresholds the two rise and fall together (Spearman $\rho=0.99$). A single-pendulum label is thus learnable to the extent that it marks the center of the hump, which the early state fixes. Only at 15\%, read more than a swing after the event, does v2 clearly beat that predictor (91.1\% against 85.3\%), having learned something about the label beyond where the hump forms.

Second, a single-pendulum label reliably marks the hump only at thresholds that are passed close to the event. From 3\% to 5\%, the label fires a median of at most two time units from the first pendulum over the top and lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in 98.9--99.4\% of runs, and v2 places 99.1--99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ of its own label, as it does on the hump label, though with a larger mean distance (0.34--0.40 against 0.27); labeling the first pendulum over the top directly gives 98.9\%. When the label is read later, at a threshold that the pendulums on the flanks of the hump can also reach, which pendulum crosses first depends on the moment in the swing at which the threshold is passed, because the hump holds its energy in a different form at each moment.

To see how, we integrated the test runs again and, at the sample at which each label fires, split the energy of every pendulum, Eq.~(\ref{eq:energy}), into its four parts. Once the first pendulum has gone over the top, the pendulums of the hump swing over the top and back together. Near the bottom of the uniform swing, in the middle quarter of a half period, about seven of them lie beyond the top, the one labeled at 10\% by about a full turn, and they move slowly: four-fifths of that pendulum's energy is held by the global coupling, whose energy $\htl(\theta_n-\bar\theta)^2/2$ grows with the square of a pendulum's angle from the ring average. This twist is largest for the pendulum that has turned furthest, at the center, so the energy peaks there. The center holds a median 10.3\% of the total, against 7.1--7.6\% two sites to either side, and the 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the center in 94\% of the runs in which it fires near the bottom of the swing. In the quarter around a turning point, the same pendulums have swung back below the top and move fast. Nine-tenths of the labeled pendulum's energy is then kinetic, and the energy is spread almost evenly over five pendulums, 9.2\% at the center and 9.4--10.0\% one and two sites from it, before it falls off. Which of the five crosses 10\% first is decided by small differences in speed: in the 36\% of runs whose 10\% label fires near a turning point, it lies within $\pm1$ of the center in only 32\%, most often two sites from it, at the edge of the hump's flat top. The springs only choose the side. They hold a few percent of the labeled pendulum's energy, and splitting each spring's energy evenly leaves the contrast nearly unchanged (92\% and 34\%). It merely spreads these misses evenly over both sides, whereas with each pendulum owning the spring to its right they fall mostly on the right (45\% two sites to the right, 8\% to the left), which is why the first-crossing label tends to lie to the right of the hump center and of the swing-averaged label [Fig.~\ref{fig:jitter}(a)].

The label therefore does not simply get worse the later it fires. Since the first pendulum goes over the top within a quarter of a half period after a turning point in 96\% of runs, the moment in the swing at which a later label fires is set largely by its delay after the event, and the share of runs whose 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center rises and falls with each half swing: it is 30\% for crossings 3.5 time units after the event (near the next turning point), 99\% at 5.5 (near the bottom of the swing), 19\% at 7.5 and 85\% at 9. Labels passed close to the event escape this, because the hump's energy has not yet spread over its top. When the 5\% label fires near a turning point, the energy still falls off from the center, which holds 5.1\% against 4.1\% two sites off, and the label lies within $\pm1$ of the center in 99\% of the 3\% of runs that reach 5\% there, and in 98\% of those that reach it two to four time units after the event, near the next turning point, against 28\% for the 10\% label. The first pendulum over the top, which is picked by its angle rather than its energy, likewise lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in 99\% of the 62\% of runs in which it goes over in the quarter around a turning point rather than later in the swing. Over all runs, the 10\% label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in only 63\% (79\% once the center is shifted by one site, as for the predictor above), and v2's accuracy on it, 77.1\%, is the lowest of all the thresholds.

At 15\%, the label lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center again in 85\% of runs. When it fires 6 to 12 time units after the event, as it does in 56\% of runs, it lies within $\pm1$ of the center in 99\% of them, whether near a turning point or not. By then the hump has narrowed: when the 15\% label fires, the center holds a median 15.4\% of the energy and the pendulums two sites off 8.6--8.7\%, so no pendulum on a flank comes close. It misses mostly in the 16\% of runs that reach 15\% only 14 or more time units after the event, where it lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in only 25\% and five or more sites from it in half; on these runs v2 places 55\% within $\pm1$ of its label, which accounts for most of its gain over the hump center as a predictor.

The hump label depends far less on when it is read [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(b)], since its one-swing average takes in both the moments at which the hump holds its energy in the twist and those at which it holds it in motion, and it sums three pendulums rather than picking one. With thresholds of 10\%, 15\% and 20\% in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), whose one-swing averages end a median of 3, 5 and 7 time units after the event, v2 places 99.4\%, 99.4\% and 98.0\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, whereas the first crossings of 7\%, 10\% and 12\%, read a median of 3, 5.5 and 7.5 time units after the event, give 92.9\%, 77.1\% and 83.7\%. This average is why the threshold of 15\% in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), chosen only so that the hump label fires with the first-crossing label, did no harm, whereas a single-pendulum label needs a threshold that is passed close to the event.

The Floquet filter, which is the same for every label, rises and falls with v2 across the thresholds ($\rho=0.93$), from 52.0\% at 10\% to 72.6\% at 4\%, and v1 places 88.5\% and 88.9\% of runs within $\pm1$ at 4\% and 5\%, against 60.1\% at 10\% (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}). The best threshold for learning is thus not arbitrary: it marks the first pendulum going over the top. The most accurate, 4\%, is about 2.4\,$E_{\mathrm{sep}}$, with 3\% and 5\% within 0.3 points of it, and the accuracy published in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} was obtained at an effective threshold in this range, 4--5\% (Appendix~\ref{sec:repro}). Before training, we had also fixed a rule for choosing a threshold with physical meaning: the smallest share of the total energy whose label fires no earlier than the event in at least 95\% of validation runs and lies within $\pm1$ of the hump center in at least 98\%. None of the shares we computed passed. The 4\% label fires before the event in a quarter of the runs and the 5\% label at or after it in only 94.5\%, while from 6\% on the label marks the hump center too rarely (95.9\% of runs at 6\%). Of the other single-pendulum labels we computed, the first crossings of 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6\,$E_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and the first pendulum over the top, only the latter and, narrowly, the first crossing of 3\,$E_{\mathrm{sep}}$, about 5.1\% of the total energy, passed. A threshold on one pendulum's share of the energy thus works only insofar as it fires at the event, and on rings of other sizes the same share means something else (Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}). We therefore use the sweep to explain the target rather than to define it, and keep 10\% only for the comparisons with v1.

Instead, we let the event itself time the hump label. At the moment the first pendulum goes over the top, we average the symmetric site energy over the swing centered on that moment and name the center of the three neighboring pendulums that hold the most energy. This \emph{event-timed hump label} has no energy threshold: it fires at a physical event, its window is one swing, and three pendulums is the narrowest window that finds the center of a flat-topped hump. It lies within $\pm1$ of the hump label of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) in 99.6\% of test runs, and v2 places 99.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ of it, as on that label, with a mean distance of 0.28 against 0.27 (Table~\ref{tab:labels}), a difference that vanishes when v2 is trained on both labels side by side (0.28 each). Once the label averages over a swing, neither its window nor its timing matters much [Fig.~\ref{fig:threshold}(b)]. Windows of five and seven pendulums give 99.5--99.6\%, whether timed by the event or by thresholds of 10--20\% in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), and the window of three falls only at 20\% (98.0\%), where its average ends a median of seven time units after the event, presumably because in some runs the hump has moved by then: most of the extra misses are by two or three sites (99.3\% within $\pm3$, against 99.6\% at 15\%). Before these runs we had fixed a rule: the event-timed label would replace that of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) unless, on the validation pool, it lost more than 0.3 points within $\pm1$ or its mean distance grew by more than 0.03 sites. It gained 0.03 points at the same mean distance to within 0.001 sites, and it is our recommended target; since it agrees so closely with the label of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}), the results obtained on the latter carry over.

\subsection{How the settings enter}
\label{sec:settings}

The threshold was not the only setting of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} fixed by hand; so were the range of amplitudes, the size of the offsets, the number of pendulums and the couplings. We asked of each what it means physically, using further pools at fixed settings (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}) and training v2 on the event-timed hump label at each.

The spectrum sets the clock. To separate the growth rate from everything else that changes with the amplitude, we simulated runs at eight fixed amplitudes between 1.60 and 1.95, over which $\sigma_1$ rises from 0.042 to 0.183 and the number of growing modes from two to seven. The first pendulum goes over the top after a median of 120 time units at the lowest amplitude and 33 at the highest, yet this time multiplied by $\sigma_1$ stays between 5.0 and 6.0 [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(a)]. Localization thus takes 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode at any amplitude (median 5.75 over a pool spanning the whole interval). This is of the order of the $\ln(1.4/0.002)\approx6.6$ $e$-foldings that a single growing mode needs to rise from the size the offsets give it, about 0.002~rad, to the 1.4~rad that carries a pendulum over the top, consistent with the picture of localization as a modulational instability followed by nonlinear focusing \cite{dauxois1993energy,daumont1997modulational}. The amplitudes of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are best described as growth rates of 0.075--0.153. \emph{When} the energy localizes is therefore set largely by the amplitude, as the amplitude dependence of the localization time in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} already suggested: v2's time head predicts the localization time to a median error of 1.5\%, but the amplitude alone predicts it to 5.0\%, leaving a gain of only about two time units. \emph{Where} it localizes is the real prediction problem.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig_clock.pdf}
  \caption{The growth spectrum sets the clock and the coarse site (test pools). (a)~Median time at which the first pendulum goes over the top, at eight fixed amplitudes (labels) and for chains at global couplings $\htl=0.3$--0.7 (diamonds), against the $e$-folding time of the fastest mode; the line is $5.75/\sigma_1$. (b)~Median delay of that time when the offsets of the same runs are scaled by $s$, against the prediction $\ln(1/s)/\sigma_1$, in five amplitude bins. (c)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label of Sec.~\ref{sec:target} for the Floquet filter (filled) and for v2 trained on each condition (open; three seeds) against the size of the offsets relative to the distance above threshold, for fixed amplitudes, for amplitude bins of the rescaled pools, and for the twin chains at $\htl=0.4$ and 0.6 (diamonds, with their own $A_c$). (d)~Share of runs whose site lies within $\pm1$ of that of the run with the same offsets at $\htl=0.5$ and $A=1.65$, 1.75 or 1.85 (marker shape), against the rms difference of the growth rates of modes 1--12 in percent of $\sigma_1$: chains at $\htl=0.5$ and other amplitudes, the twins at $\htl=0.4$ and 0.6, chains at those couplings that match only $\sigma_1$, and the closest chains at $\htl=0.3$ and 0.7.}
  \label{fig:clock}
\end{figure}

The offsets, the scatter of the release, are part of the physics rather than noise: since the uniform swing is an exact solution of Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}), without them nothing would localize. Scaling the offsets of the same runs by a factor $s$ between 1/8 and 4 should shift the localization time by $\ln(1/s)/\sigma_1$, and the measured delays follow this with a slope of 1.10 [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(b)], the effective growth being slightly slower than that of the fastest mode, as we find again for sensor noise in Sec.~\ref{sec:realchain}. The size of the offsets also moves the site: between the stated offsets and an eighth of them, it stays in place in only 37\% of runs. With smaller offsets the growing modes need longer to rise, while the modes that do not grow keep their size, since the Floquet multipliers of a stable mode of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) lie on the unit circle \cite{magnus1966hill}, so that their local detail weighs less when the hump forms. Linear theory reaches correspondingly further. The Floquet filter predicts the event-timed hump label within $\pm1$ in 52\% of runs at four times the offsets, 73\% at the stated ones and 87\% at an eighth, and across amplitudes its accuracy falls as the largest offset $\eta_{\max}$ grows relative to the distance above threshold, from 89--99\% where $\eta_{\max}/(A-A_c)$ is below 0.04 to 25--35\% where it is about one [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(c)]. Close to the threshold, where the modes grow slowly, the filter also needs more swings to pick the fastest one out (15 periods at $A=1.60$, against four from $A=1.85$ up). A network trained on each condition, by contrast, places at least 98.4\% of runs within $\pm1$, learning what linear theory misses.

The number of pendulums sets how many modes compete. At $A=1.75$ every wave longer than about 18 pendulums grows, so a longer ring samples the same band more finely: it holds about $N/18$ growing modes, while the fastest rate barely changes, from 0.113 at $N=50$ to 0.120 at $N=400$. We simulated rings of 50, 200 and 400 pendulums at the amplitudes and offsets of the main pools and trained a wider version of v2 on each, with two more dilated layers (dilations 64 and 128) so that every pendulum sees a stretch of 513 pendulums, and used this wider network at $N=100$ too. From 50 to 400 pendulums, the number of growing modes rises from two to 22, and the share of runs in which, when the first pendulum goes over the top, a rival hump at least five sites away holds at least half as much energy rises from 2.4\% to 71\% (20\% at $N=100$). The first pendulum also goes over the top somewhat sooner on longer rings, though still after 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode (6.0 at $N=50$, 5.3 at $N=400$), presumably because, with more crests growing, the largest of them starts out larger. The Floquet filter falls from 77.6\% to 66.0\% within $\pm1$, yet the wider network only from 99.9\% to 98.8\%, its far misses rising from 0.1\% to 0.9\%: on a longer ring, linear theory misses more of the competition between growing crests, but the network still reads its outcome from the early state, consistent with the hump forming where the growing band focuses the energy, as in the modulational instability of discrete lattices \cite{kivshar1992modulational}.

A share of the total energy, on the other hand, means something different on every ring. The first crossing of 10\% comes a median of 2 time units after the event at $N=50$, 5.5 at $N=100$ and 20.5 at $N=200$, where it lies within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label in only 49\% of the runs in which it fires; even the hump label of Eq.~(\ref{eq:hump}) does so in only 82\% there. At $N=400$, where 10\% is 40 times one pendulum's share, the first crossing of 10\% had fired in only 2.9\% of test runs by the time we stopped integrating, which was a median of 32.5 time units after the event (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}); that of 4\% came a median of 8.5 time units after the event and lay within $\pm1$ of the event-timed hump label in only 41\% of the runs in which it fired. The event itself is the same on every ring.

Last among the settings taken over from Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} are the couplings. The neighbor coupling $\gt$ barely changes the long waves (Sec.~\ref{sec:realchain}), but the global coupling adds the same stiffness to every mode in Eq.~(\ref{eq:hill}) and so shifts the whole spectrum: the threshold moves from $A_c=1.38$ at $\htl=0.4$ to 1.78 at $\htl=0.6$, where a chain released at $A=1.75$ would not localize at all. If a chain entered the problem only through its growth spectrum, a change of $\htl$ could be undone by a change of amplitude. For $A=1.65$, 1.75 and 1.85 at $\htl=0.5$ we therefore chose the amplitudes at $\htl=0.4$ and 0.6 whose growth rates differ least from these, by 2--6\% of $\sigma_1$ (1.46--1.66 and 1.85--2.04), and released these twin chains from exactly the same offsets as their references. They localize after 5.4--5.8 $e$-foldings [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(a)], have a rival hump as often as their references to within 3 points, and the Floquet filter, computed with each chain's own $\htl$ and $A_c$, falls on the same curve [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(c)]. Run by run, the site lies within $\pm1$ of the reference run's in 88--98\% of runs, against 81--93\% for the closest chains at $\htl=0.3$ and 0.7, 5--13\% away in spectrum, and 77--91\% for chains at 0.4 and 0.6 that share only the fastest rate [Fig.~\ref{fig:clock}(d)]: the whole spectrum, not its fastest rate alone, decides where the energy goes. We had predicted that the twins would agree with their references at least as often as chains at $\htl=0.5$ whose amplitude differs by 0.025, 5--17\% away in spectrum; this holds at 1.65 and 1.75 and fails by up to 1.5 points at 1.85.

The spectrum does not decide the last pendulum, however. At $A=1.75$, chains whose amplitude differs by 0.01, 3\% away in spectrum, keep the exact site in 83--84\% of runs, the twins, 3--4\% away, in 62--73\%. The difference lies in the modes that do not grow. Since the swing is symmetric in time about the release, every monodromy matrix has equal diagonal elements \cite{magnus1966hill}, so that after $n$ swings a growing mode has responded to an initial offset by exactly $\cosh[n\sigma_mT(A)]$, which depends on the chain only through $\sigma_m$, whereas a stable mode has turned by an angle per swing that depends on the amplitude and the coupling separately (for mode 7, 0.60 and 0.98~rad in the twins of $A=1.75$, against 0.79). Linear theory accordingly shows the same gap: at $A=1.75$ and 1.85 the evolved offsets of twin chains peak within $\pm1$ of their references' in 71--94\% of runs, against 94--99\% for amplitude shifts of 0.01. The global coupling thus enters the clock, the competition between humps and the coarse site through the growth spectrum alone, and the last pendulum also through the modes that do not grow.

\subsection{Toward a real chain}
\label{sec:realchain}

A real chain will be observed with noisy sensors, and its parameters will be known only approximately. Since an error of $10^{-3}$~rad in the initial state already moves a quarter of the labels (Sec.~\ref{sec:physics}), let us first look at sensor noise. We trained the network on camera-like data, eight angle frames 0.5 time units apart with Gaussian noise on every pendulum and frame, starting the observation at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 or 30. Watching from release, the camera does well up to about $10^{-3}$~rad and degrades beyond. Noise first causes far misses: the share within $\pm1$ hardly changes at first, while the share of far misses triples. Noise picks the wrong hump before it blurs the right one.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig6_noise.pdf}
  \caption{Waiting divides the sensor noise by the growth of the unstable modes. (a)~Mean distance of the camera setup (first-crossing label; one seed per cell) against the sensor noise $\sigma_s$ divided by the growth of the fastest mode since release, for observations starting at $\tau=0$, 10, 20 and 30; the horizontal line is the noise-free error from release. (b)~Waiting per tenfold noise for the camera in four amplitude bins, on the first-crossing and swing-averaged labels (dots, fits; bars, 95\% intervals), against the predictions from the mean growth rate of the growing modes and from the fastest mode.}
  \label{fig:noise}
\end{figure}

Waiting helps, because the growing modes rise above the sensor noise while the noise does not grow. If the fastest mode alone set the pace, each tenfold increase in sensor noise would cost $\ln10/\sigma_1$, about 20 time units of waiting, and this was our initial prediction. Figure~\ref{fig:noise} shows that waiting pays off more slowly. The camera's error depends on the noise and the start time essentially through the noise relative to the grown signal [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(a)], but each tenfold increase in noise costs about 25 time units, close to what the mean growth rate of the growing modes gives rather than the fastest one. A likely reason is that white noise enters every ring mode equally, while the site depends on all the growing modes, each of which rises above the noise at its own rate. Having found this on the first-crossing label, we predicted from the mean growth rate 24.8 time units for the swing-averaged label before any later-start run on that label had finished, and measured 25.5. Split by amplitude, the waiting cost falls as the growth rates rise [Fig.~\ref{fig:noise}(b)]. In practice, a camera ten times coarser than $10^{-3}$~rad catches up with a precise one if it starts watching about 25 time units later, which for 20~cm pendulums still leaves about 3.6~s of warning.

Fewer sensors cost less than one might fear. Tracking every second pendulum costs nothing, with or without noise, and every fourth costs little without noise. Every eighth fails, however. Its 13 sensors satisfy the Nyquist criterion for the five growing modes, which we had expected to suffice, but at release the stable modes hold about 90\% of the perturbation, and on 13 sensors they alias onto the wavenumbers of the growing ones. One camera tracking every second pendulum to $10^{-3}$~rad, with v2's ten frames from release rather than the eight of the noise grid, scores a mean distance of 1.93 on the first-crossing label, well ahead of v1 with perfect data (3.14), and locates the forming hump within $\pm1$ in 96.8\% of runs. For 20~cm pendulums, $10^{-3}$~rad is 0.2~mm at the bob; we estimate, but have not tested, that one camera at 30--60 frames per second tracking markers on the bobs can reach it.

  \centering

Mean distance on the first-crossing label, over the runs that localize by $\tau=150$: nearly all, except at $\htl$ $+10\%$, where 80\% do. The last column describes the growth spectrum at $A=1.75$.}
  \label{tab:robust}
  \small
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lrrl@{}}
    \toprule
    Test condition & v1 & v2 & Growth spectrum at $A=1.75$ \\
    \midrule
    Nominal chain & 3.14 & 1.49 & 5 growing modes, $\sigma_1=0.1185$ \\
    Neighbor coupling $\gt$ $\pm10\%$ & 3.26 / 3.39 & 1.97 / 1.97 & essentially unchanged \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $-10\%$ & 4.36 & 4.25 & $\sigma_1$ $+21\%$; 6 modes grow; $A_c=1.48$ \\
    Global coupling $\htl$ $+10\%$ & 5.91 & 5.53 & $\sigma_1$ $-33\%$; 3 modes grow; $A_c=1.68$ \\
    One pendulum 2~mm longer & 18.9 & 22.9 & the impurity attracts the site \\

The parameters of a real chain will also be off. We applied both networks, trained on the nominal chain, to shifted ones (Table~\ref{tab:robust}), and the damage again follows the Floquet spectrum. A 10\% error in the neighbor coupling, which leaves the spectrum essentially unchanged, costs v2 about half a site. A 10\% error in the global coupling, by contrast, changes how fast and how many modes grow, and both networks fall to 4--6 sites, which erases most of v2's lead; $\htl$ must therefore be known to a few percent. As found in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, an impurity strongly attracts the localization. A single pendulum about 2~mm longer, whose restoring term in Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}) is therefore 1\% weaker, pins the site within $\pm3$ of it in 92\% of runs and misleads both networks, which have never seen such a cue. Retrained on chains with one random pendulum up to 2\% weaker, v2 finds it from the motion alone, since a longer pendulum swings slightly slower, and reaches a mean distance of 1.06.

Real pendulums also lose energy, and the missing damping was the main gap we saw between our simulations and a real chain. With linear damping the uniform swing decays toward the threshold $A_c$, so a run localizes only if its perturbation has grown enough before then. At a quality factor $Q\ge1{,}000$ almost every run still localizes, at $Q\approx330$ only 71\% do, and at $Q=100$ none do; integrating the Floquet growth rate along the decaying swing predicts the delay. Retrained on damped chains, v2 even improves with damping, to 0.84 at $Q\approx330$ on the runs that localize, presumably because near threshold fewer and longer modes grow and the site depends less on local detail; these are not simply the easy runs, since without damping v2 does worse on them than on the rest. Here v1's binary ``localizes'' head (Sec.~\ref{sec:inputs}) becomes useful: from the first 4.5 time units it tells whether a run will localize at all, correctly in 99.5\% of damped runs.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{paper_fig_training.pdf}
  \caption{What a network must be trained on (event-timed hump label, test pools, three seeds). (a)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ at fixed amplitudes for networks trained at that amplitude, over 1.60--1.95, and over 1.65--1.85 (band); arrows mark values below the axis. (b)~Accuracy within $\pm1$ (\%, seed means) of the wider network of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, trained on rings of 50, 100, 200 and 400 pendulums, and of v2, trained at $N=100$ (rows), on rings of 50--400 pendulums (columns). Outlined: the ring a network was trained on. Asterisks: shorter rings whose size divides that of the training ring, on which a circular CNN computes what it would on the training ring with the state repeated around that ring.}
  \label{fig:training}
\end{figure}

These tests applied a network to conditions it had not seen. To find out what a network must be trained on, we also trained the recipe on the event-timed hump label at fixed amplitudes, at other offset sizes, at other global couplings and on rings of other sizes (Fig.~\ref{fig:training}). A network trained at a single amplitude places 99.5--99.7\% of runs within $\pm1$ from 1.65 to 1.95, and one trained over the whole interval does as well to within 0.6 points, so a narrower range of amplitudes, which one might expect to make the problem easier, makes little difference. Only just above the threshold, at $A=1.60$, where the outcome changes steeply with the amplitude, does the network trained there gain (98.7\% against 85.8\%). Nor does a network extrapolate. The one trained on 1.65--1.85 places 90\% of runs within $\pm1$ at 1.90, 50\% at 1.95 and 25\% at 1.60, and the one trained at the stated offsets places 93\% at twice the offsets and 65\% at four times, where networks trained at those sizes reach 99.3\% and 99.1\%.

Nor does matching the spectrum let a network carry over to another coupling. Trained on the twin chains of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings}, v2 places 99.3--99.7\% of runs within $\pm1$, as on their references, but a network trained on one of two twins places only 2--55\% of the other's runs within $\pm1$, with large differences between seeds, although their sites mostly coincide. Even the network trained over 1.60--1.95 at $\htl=0.5$ places only 23--47\% of runs within $\pm1$ on the twins whose amplitudes lie in that interval. Since the uniform swing does not depend on $\htl$ (Sec.~\ref{sec:floquet}), this network reads a twin as a chain at $\htl=0.5$ with the same amplitude, and it predicts where such a chain, released from the same offsets, localizes: within $\pm1$ in 98--99\% of runs. The twin itself localizes there in only 23--47\% of runs, within half a point of how often the network is right. A network trained at one coupling thus ignores the coupling altogether, and must be trained at the chain's own.

We scored the wider network of Sec.~\ref{sec:settings} and v2 on rings of 50 to 400 pendulums [Fig.~\ref{fig:training}(b)], including new test pools of 80 and 150 pendulums (Sec.~\ref{sec:pools}). Trained on 200 and 400 pendulums, the wider network keeps 98.9\% and 95.3\% of runs within $\pm1$ at $N=100$, against 99.5\% for the one trained there. Such a transfer, however, does not test whether a network carries over to rings of other sizes, since on a ring whose size divides that of its training ring a circular CNN computes exactly what it would on its training ring with the state repeated around that ring. The repeated state is a state of the training ring, but not one the network met in training, with only every second, fourth, fifth or eighth of the ring's modes excited. The more often it repeats, the further the network falls below its score on its own ring: by less than a point when it repeats twice, 4 to 6 points when it repeats four or five times, and 16 points when the state of 50 pendulums repeats eight times around the ring of 400. On rings whose size does not divide that of its training ring, the wider network carries over only when trained on 400 pendulums, keeping 98\% at $N=150$, the one such ring we tested. Trained on 50 to 200 pendulums, it places at most 62\% of runs within $\pm1$ on such rings, and trained at $N=100$, only 17\%, 13\%, 30\% and 14\% at $N=80$, 150, 200 and 400, although it sees the whole of each. The failures of the networks trained on 100 and 200 pendulums come with large differences between seeds, whereas the one trained on 50 fails with every seed. Our expectation that seeing the whole ring would let a network carry over to rings of other sizes was thus wrong.

By contrast, v2 itself, trained at $N=100$ on the same label, keeps 97.4\% at $N=80$, against 99.4\% on its own ring; on longer rings it falls to 94.3\% at $N=150$ and then only gradually, to 92.3\% and 89.5\% at $N=200$ and 400, its far misses rising from 0.4\% on its own ring to 4.1\% at $N=150$ and 9.5\% at $N=400$. Trained on the same pools with the same recipe, it differs from the wider network only in lacking the layers with dilations of 64 and 128. These dilations exceed half of the 100-pendulum ring (there, a shift by 128 is a shift by 28), so that those layers connect pendulums in a way specific to that ring, whereas each layer of v2, with dilations of at most 32, connects them in the same way on any ring of more than 64 pendulums. The failures of the wider network trained at $N=100$ thus point to how its dilations wrap around that ring, rather than to its having learned the ring's five growing modes, which v2, seeing the whole ring too, could have learned as well.

The other training rings fit this reading: the dilations of 32, 64 and 128 all exceed half of the 50-pendulum ring, that of 128 exceeds half of the 200-pendulum ring, and none exceeds half of the 400-pendulum ring, the only training ring from which the network carries over to a ring whose size does not divide it. What matters seems to be whether a dilation exceeds half of the ring a network was trained on rather than of the ring it is tested on: trained on 400 pendulums, the network carries over to $N=150$, although its dilation of 128 exceeds half of that ring, and trained on 100, it fails at $N=400$, where none of its dilations does. Two caveats remain. The two extra layers also widen the view from 129 to 513 pendulums, which goes 10, 5 and 2.6 times around the training rings of 50, 100 and 200 pendulums but only 1.3 times around that of 400, as the view of v2 does around its own ring. Since a view spans about four times the largest dilation, it goes more than twice around a ring just when that dilation exceeds half of the ring, so that we cannot tell layers that reach more than halfway around the training ring from a view that goes around it more than twice. And the networks trained on other rings have also seen fewer or more growing modes and rival humps, so that only the comparison at $N=100$ isolates the two extra layers.

The loss of v2 on longer rings may come from the competition between their many growing modes, which it never saw, or from its view of 129 pendulums, which no longer spans these rings; our data cannot separate the two. That the loss beyond $N=150$ is only gradual suggests that most of what decides the site lies within the pendulums that v2 sees, perhaps because the band of growing waves is cut off at the same wavelength on every ring, about 18 pendulums at $A=1.75$, so that on rings of 150 to 400 pendulums only one to three of their 8 to 22 growing modes are longer than its view. Neither candidate accounts for the two points that v2 loses at $N=80$, a ring it sees whole and on which fewer modes grow, so that part of its loss on longer rings may come from neither. Whether a network trained on a long ring needs to see all of it, we have not tested.

A network for a real chain must therefore be trained at that chain's global coupling, over the amplitudes at which the chain will be released, at its release scatter, and on a ring of the chain's size.

\FloatBarrier
\section{Conclusions}
\label{sec:conclusions}

In this study we revisited the prediction of where a noise-seeded type-III instability localizes energy in a sine-Gordon pendulum ring, starting this time from the physics of the instability rather than from the data. The Floquet growth spectrum of the uniform swing explains much of what was found empirically before. Only a handful of the longest ring modes grow, and this sets the optimal width of the box-car smoothing of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}. The outcome is deterministic, so prediction is limited by how precisely the initial state is measured rather than by chaos, and the coarse answer lives in the amplitudes and phases of the few growing modes. The spectrum also sets the clock: localization takes 5--6 $e$-foldings of the fastest mode at any amplitude and global coupling, each halving of the release scatter adds about $\ln2/\sigma_1$, and linear theory locates the site the better, the smaller the offsets are compared with the distance above threshold. A change of the global coupling can be undone by a change of amplitude that restores the spectrum, for the clock and, in 88--98\% of runs, for the site to within a pendulum; only the last pendulum depends also on the modes that do not grow. A longer ring samples the same band of growing waves more finely, so that more modes and rival humps compete, yet the site remains almost as predictable.

The same spectrum guided the design of the neural predictor. Since little grows or travels during the observation window while the growing modes span the whole ring, the network must see the whole ring, and once it does, the recurrent layer of v1 is not needed. Since the dynamics are the same at every pendulum, the network should apply the same filters everywhere and score every pendulum the same way. A circular CNN built on these principles, with a thousandth of the parameters, halves the error of the CNN-BiLSTM, beats it with 60 times less training data, and barely overfits. To answer the question left open in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the features that decide the localization site are largely the projections of the early state onto the few growing long waves, with local detail deciding the last site or two.

The target deserves as much care as the model. The first pendulum to hold 10\% of the energy is the instantaneous peak of a breathing hump about eight pendulums wide, and most of the remaining error on that label is its own jitter; defined at the scale of the hump, the label fires just as early and is located within $\pm1$ in 99.4\% of runs. The threshold need not be arbitrary either. Trained on the first crossing of any threshold from 3\% to 12\% of the energy, the network learns essentially where the hump forms, but the label reliably marks the hump only at thresholds that, like 3--5\%, are passed close to the moment the first pendulum swings over the top. The 10\% of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, read about five time units later, depends on the phase of the swing, naming a pendulum at the edge of the hump whenever the hump holds its energy in motion rather than in the twist of its turned pendulums, and is the hardest to learn. Timing the hump label by the first pendulum going over the top leaves the target without any energy threshold, at no cost in accuracy, and unlike a share of the total energy, this event means the same on a ring of any size. For a real chain, sensor noise can be traded against warning time at a cost set by the mean growth rate of the unstable modes, and in simulation one camera tracking every second pendulum already beats v1 with perfect data. A network must, however, be trained at the chain's global coupling, over the chain's amplitudes and release scatter, and on a ring of the chain's size: it takes a chain at another coupling for one at the coupling it was trained at, does not extrapolate in amplitude or to larger offsets, and does not carry over reliably to a ring of another size.

These conclusions have limits. The comparison with v1 was made at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, close to the threshold at which the first-crossing label is hardest to learn; at the lower threshold and smaller offsets of its published accuracy the gap narrows, to 92.5\% against 99.4\% within $\pm1$. Damping was simulated as linear, sensor noise as white, and impurities as a single lengthened pendulum, whereas a real chain will have small differences at every pendulum and correlated measurement errors. Testing the recommended setup on a bench-top chain is the natural next step.
