\appendix

\section{Training details}
\label{app:training}

\textit{v1.} Implemented as described in Sec.~\ref{sec:predictors}, with the defaults of the TensorFlow (Keras) layers used in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} (26,499,205 parameters; Adam \cite{kingma2015adam} at a learning rate of $10^{-3}$, batch size 64, early stopping on the validation loss); training takes about 23 minutes. Some seeds never leave the loss of a uniform guess, $\ln100$, and these were repeated with another seed and are not scored: one of three at the stated settings, one of nine in the threshold study at the stated offsets, and 11 of 14 at offsets of $\pm0.0125$, presumably because the deviations that locate the hotspot are then smaller against the spread of amplitudes.

\textit{v2.} Hidden activations are GELUs \cite{hendrycks2016gelu}, and the per-site head is a circular convolution of kernel 3, a GELU and a $1\times1$ convolution. Training uses AdamW (learning rate $3\times10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$) with a cosine decay and 3\% warmup, batch size 256, for 7,050 steps (30 epochs of 60,000 runs), keeping the checkpoint with the lowest validation mean distance, evaluated every 235 steps on 5,000 validation runs. The architecture comparison used the same budget. Screening runs had 15 epochs and three seeds (two for an unknown start, one per cell of the noise and sensor grids), so differences below about 0.1 sites there are within noise. The mirror image of a run maps pendulum $n$ to $N-1-n$, and its first-crossing label is the mirror image of the label computed with left-hand springs. Damping adds a term $-\gamma\dot\theta_n$ to Eq.~(\ref{eq:eom}), so that a free pendulum has quality factor $Q=1/\gamma$; every threshold is then a fraction of the energy the chain still holds.

\textit{Hardware.} Most networks were trained on one laptop (an Apple M3 Pro, mostly on its built-in GPU), and about a hundred in the threshold and settings studies on a cloud GPU (an NVIDIA L40).

\section{The settings behind the published accuracy}
\label{sec:repro}

We implemented the CNN-BiLSTM of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} in PyTorch with the defaults of the TensorFlow (Keras) layers used there; given the weights of the original Keras model, it has the same 26,499,205 parameters and gives the same outputs. Its data come from a simulator that gives the same localization site and time as the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} on 1,000 of 1,000 test runs, and the only deliberate change is that the input scaler is fitted on the training pool alone. Trained at the settings stated in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand}, the network places 61.7\% and 59.1\% of test runs within $\pm1$ in two seeds, with mean distances of 3.00 and 3.27, against the published 94.4\% and 1.44; a third seed never trained.

The published accuracy belongs to other settings (Table~\ref{tab:repro}). The first-crossing label at 10\% fires about five time units after the first pendulum swings over the top, by which time the pendulum that crosses first depends on the phase of the swing (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}). Retrained on first-crossing labels at 4\% and 5\% of the total energy, which still mark the center of the hump (Sec.~\ref{sec:target}), and otherwise unchanged, the network places 88.5\% and 88.9\% of runs within $\pm1$. The offsets were also smaller than stated: the data-generation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} sets a noise level of 0.025, and its simulation code applies a noise level $s$ as offsets $s\,(U-\tfrac12)$ with $U\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$, so that the training data had offsets $\eta_n\sim\mathcal{U}(-0.0125,0.0125)$. At a threshold of 4\% and these offsets the network reaches 92.5\% within $\pm1$ and a mean distance of 1.69, close to the published 94.4\% and 1.44, although at such small offsets most seeds never leave the loss of a uniform guess (Appendix~\ref{app:training}). The accuracies published in Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} were thus obtained with an effective threshold of 4--5\% of the total energy and offsets of $\pm0.0125$. To measure the gain of the new design at the settings stated there, every comparison with v1 in this paper uses the 10\% threshold and offsets of $\pm0.025$, at which v1 places 60.4\% of runs within $\pm1$ and v2 77.2\% (Table~\ref{tab:headline}); at the settings of the published accuracy v2 reaches 99.4\%. The few remaining points where the published description and the simulation code of Ref.~\cite{mittal2026jand} differ, such as the time axes of its figures, which count samples of 0.5 time units, are listed in the report that accompanies our code.
